topic: How a bank collapse brought down Paraguay's president Santiago Peña

sources.title: How a bank collapse in Paraguay brought down the country’s President | Explained
sources.text:
How a bank collapse in Paraguay brought down the country’s President | Explained
Millions of customers, abruptly, lost access to their savings accounts and pension payments after regulators seized the bank, setting off a sequence of events that culminated in a change of political leadership
People protest outside the home of Paraguay's ousted President Santiago Pena, who was placed under house arrest on suspicion of breach of trust following his removal by the Senate as prosecutors investigate the collapse of Ueno Bank, in Asuncion, Paraguay, on November 6, 2026.
| Photo Credit: AP
The story so far: Following impeachment proceedings initiated against the country’s President Santiago Pena, Paraguay’s Senate voted to remove him for misconduct in office and placed him under house arrest on November 7. Subsequently, Vice-President Pedro Alliana was sworn in as interim President.
Both Mr. Alliana and Mr. Pena belong to the Colorado Party, the dominant force in Paraguayan politics since the 1940s.

sources.title: Ueno Bank Collapse Costs Paraguay's Santiago Peña His Presidency
sources.text:
- Paraguay's Senate impeached and removed President Santiago Peña, with all 44 senators present voting in favour.
- Peña was placed under house arrest as prosecutors investigate alleged misconduct linked to the Ueno Bank collapse.
- Vice-President Pedro Alliana was sworn in as president amid investigations and growing pressure over the bank's failure.
Paraguay's Senate has impeached and removed President Santiago Peña from office, placing him under house arrest as prosecutors investigate allegations of misconduct linked to the collapse of Ueno Bank, a major financial institution that held millions of customers' deposits and substantial public funds. Vice-President Pedro Alliana was sworn in as his successor on Friday, November 6, after all 44 senators present voted in favour of Peña's removal.
The impeachment followed a financial crisis that has raised questions about the government's relationship with Ueno, the use of public money and regulatory oversight of the bank. Peña had submitted his resignation a day earlier, but lawmakers proceeded with the impeachment process. He has denied wrongdoing. Alliana, meanwhile, has also come under investigation in connection with the bank, adding to the political uncertainty surrounding the change of government.
Ueno Bank Collapse Triggers Impeachment
The crisis escalated after Paraguay's Central Bank placed Ueno Bank into a resolution process on November 3, after finding that it had breached minimum solvency requirements. The intervention left customers struggling to access their deposits and conduct transactions.
Ueno had approximately 2.9 million customers, close to half Paraguay's population. According to Reuters, the bank administered around $850 million in public funds, while lawmakers accused Peña's government of allowing $355 million from the state pension fund to be deposited with the lender, beyond legal limits.
Investigators are examining Ueno's lending practices, including loans to companies connected to its owners, and whether political relationships influenced regulatory oversight.
Peña had previously held shares in Grupo Vázquez, the holding company associated with Ueno, before selling his stake in March 2025. Former Central Bank governor Carlos Carvallo, who had previously headed the financial company that preceded Ueno, has also become a subject of the investigation.
The lower house voted 78 in favour of impeaching Peña on Thursday, November 5. Although Peña submitted his resignation on Thursday, a joint session of Congress could not take it up because it lacked a quorum. The Senate proceeded with the impeachment trial on Friday, ultimately voting unanimously to remove him from office.
In his farewell message, Peña said: "I say goodbye with gratitude, without ignoring the anguish of those who are waiting for answers today."
Pedro Alliana Takes Over Amid Political Fallout
Alliana was sworn in to complete the remainder of the presidential term, which runs until August 2028. His first challenge will be addressing the financial fallout from Ueno's collapse and restoring public confidence in the banking system.
Speaking after taking office, Alliana said: "The Paraguay we receive today has urgent needs."
The government has promised compensation for affected depositors. The Central Bank has said deposit insurance of up to approximately $35,000 per customer will cover the full balances of an estimated 97 per cent of Ueno's customers. The first repayments began on Thursday, initially covering depositors with balances of up to 10 million guaraníes (approximately $1,500), according to the Associated Press.
The crisis has also exposed divisions within the ruling Colorado Party. Former president Horacio Cartes, Peña's political mentor and the party's leader, backed his removal, withdrawing support from the president he had previously helped bring to power. Cartes said the party would not support "the plundering of public and private funds and pensioners' money".
Depositors have also demanded accountability. A worker at the state electricity company, whose employee pension fund had money deposited at Ueno, told the Associated Press: "This was an enormous betrayal of trust."
The political fallout is particularly significant because Alliana himself is under investigation in connection with the bank. His appointment therefore does not bring an end to the scrutiny of the political leadership associated with Ueno.
Peña Faces Investigation After Losing Office
Peña's removal also has implications for the legal proceedings against him. Under Article 189 of Paraguay's Constitution, democratically elected former presidents are entitled to lifetime Senate seats, with parliamentary privileges, unless they have been impeached and found guilty. Peña's removal therefore stripped him of the legal protections he could have retained had his resignation been accepted.
Prosecutors are investigating suspected breach of trust, influence peddling and the alleged misuse of public office for personal gain in connection with the bank's operations. Peña has denied wrongdoing and was ordered to remain under house arrest until his appearance before prosecutors on Saturday. However, the allegations have not yet been established in court, and Peña has not been convicted of any offence.
The investigation has extended to Ueno's former executives and associates. The Associated Press reported that prosecutors had charged 27 bank officials and associates with breach of trust and attempted fraud. Former Central Bank governor Carvallo is also facing an arrest order.
With Alliana now in office, Paraguay faces two immediate challenges: ensuring that affected customers recover their deposits and establishing whether public officials were involved in the bank's financial collapse. Peña's removal has settled the question of presidential succession, but the investigation into Ueno and its political connections remains ongoing.

sources.title: Three Million Hit By Ueno Bank Collapse As Paraguay President Faces Impeachment
sources.text:
- Paraguay's Santiago Peña offered to resign, but the Senate has begun impeachment proceedings against him.
- Ueno Bank's crisis has left nearly three million customers unable to access their accounts.
- Criminal investigations are examining alleged financial irregularities, public deposits and Peña's links to the bank's owner.
Paraguayan President Santiago Peña has offered to resign after the failure of digital lender Ueno Bank left nearly three million customers unable to access their accounts, triggering protests, criminal investigations and an impeachment bid against him. However, Congress did not accept his resignation. A joint session convened to consider the offer failed to reach a quorum, while the Senate began an impeachment trial that could remove him from office.
The banking crisis has exposed the close connections between Ueno, the government and public institutions that deposited hundreds of millions of dollars with the lender. It has also raised questions about regulatory oversight, Peña's previous business ties to the bank's owner and the handling of public pension funds. While authorities have begun arrangements to return depositors' money, the president is facing a criminal investigation alongside bank executives accused of financial irregularities.
Peña Offers To Resign As Banking Crisis Triggers Political Turmoil
In a video statement posted on X on Thursday, November 5, Peña announced his decision to step down, citing the need to protect Paraguay's stability and democratic institutions.
"I have made the decision to submit my resignation as president of the republic. I do so thinking of the stability of our country, social peace and the need to preserve our democratic institutions," he said.
The lower house voted unanimously to impeach Peña shortly after his announcement. Although Congress did not accept his resignation, a joint session to consider it failed for lack of quorum. The Senate subsequently began impeachment proceedings, which could result in his removal from office. Peña has said he will cooperate with investigators and defend himself against the allegations.
The political pressure intensified after former president Horacio Cartes, the head of the ruling Colorado Party and Peña's former ally, publicly backed impeachment.
"We will not stand on the side of the theft of public, private and pensioners' funds," Cartes said, according to The Guardian.
Vice-President Pedro Alliana would succeed Peña if he left office. Resignation could also have allowed Peña to retain a lifetime Senate seat and the parliamentary immunity attached to it.
Ueno Bank Crisis Leaves Millions Without Access To Savings
The Central Bank of Paraguay initiated resolution proceedings against the lender on November 3 after finding that its solvency ratio had fallen below half the legally required minimum. The regulator attributed the shortfall to adjustments made to the bank's financial statements during the process of addressing its financial difficulties.
AP reported that Central Bank inspectors found poorly documented loans and expenses that had been incorrectly recorded as assets. Earlier inspections had also identified risky lending to companies linked to the bank's owners, including loans that exceeded legal limits and lacked sufficient collateral, as reported by Paraguayan newspaper ABC Color.
Following the intervention, Ueno's mobile application, cards and transfer services stopped working, while its branches closed. Customers were unable to access their savings, and a rush to open accounts elsewhere caused disruptions to other banks' mobile applications.
The statutory deposit guarantee covers up to 75 monthly minimum wages, equivalent to 228.3 million guaraníes per depositor, per financial institution. The Central Bank estimates that this will cover the full balances of around 97 per cent of Ueno's customers.
Congress separately authorised an advance payment of up to 40 minimum wages, or 121.76 million guaraníes, after deducting overdue debts to Ueno. The payment process is to be completed within five working days. Separately, the Central Bank began the first phase of guarantee payments for customers with deposits of up to 10 million guaraníes, no outstanding debts and an account at another financial institution.
Peña's Links To Ueno And Public Funds Under Scrutiny
The president previously held a stake in Grupo Vázquez, the business group that controls Ueno. He has said he sold his shares in March 2025 and denied having any improper role in the bank's affairs. Ueno has also maintained that Peña was never a direct shareholder or investor in the bank.
Reuters reported that Ueno administered approximately US$850 million in public funds, including money belonging to state institutions and pension-related bodies. AP separately reported that the bank held around US$800 million in public deposits as of October, approximately a quarter of its total deposits.
One of the largest exposures was that of Paraguay's Social Security Institute (IPS), which manages pension and healthcare funds for workers. Its financial manager, Gladys Vera, told ABC Color that the institution had approximately US$355 million deposited with Ueno, representing around 9 per cent of its investment portfolio.
Central bank chief Carlos Carvallo, who previously headed Ueno's predecessor Financiera Ueno, resigned on November 3 at Peña's request. The regulator said he had recused himself from decisions involving the bank.
The controversy has now extended to Peña himself. On November 5, Attorney General Emiliano Rolón Fernández opened three criminal investigations into the supervision and resolution of Ueno, the placement of public funds in the bank and the conduct of current and former government officials. The prosecutor's office said a complaint against Peña, originally filed in October 2025, had been expanded to include allegations linked to the bank's oversight and resolution. He has said he will cooperate with investigators.
Protests, Arrests And Questions Over Paraguay's Financial System
The crisis has triggered demonstrations in the capital, Asunción, with depositors, pensioners, students and workers demanding access to their money and accountability from the government.
"Santiago Peña and the Colorado Party have stolen all our savings," protester Luis Pineda told AP. "We are fed up with 70 years of plunder," he added.
Riot police used pepper spray and rubber pellets to disperse demonstrators outside Congress. Hundreds of employees of Ueno and other companies belonging to Grupo Vázquez also protested outside the Labour Ministry, demanding unpaid wages and severance payments. The Labour Ministry estimated that around 7,000 direct and indirect jobs had been affected.
The Public Prosecutor's Office charged 27 people linked to Ueno Bank and related companies with alleged offences including breach of trust, attempted fraud, improper conduct during a crisis and failure to maintain proper commercial books. Its investigation covers loans and overdrafts granted between 2025 and 2026 to companies linked to the bank. Prosecutors allege that some loans lacked sufficient collateral and that funds were transferred to other companies within the same business group.
A judge ordered six executives, including founder Miguel Vázquez and bank president Juan Manuel Gustale, into preventive detention, while two others were placed under house arrest.
Gustale's lawyer, José Fernández Zacur, disputed the allegations, telling local media: "The president or board is not responsible for deciding who receives a particular loan."

sources.title: How a digital bank’s collapse toppled Paraguay’s president
sources.text:
For years, Paraguay’s digital bank, ueno, stood out as a homegrown success story, luring roughly half the country’s people to open accounts and offering many the opportunity to hold a bank account for the very first time.
But over just five days this week, the bank collapsed, freezing the savings of nearly 3 million customers — in a country of 6.5 million people — and triggering the country’s deepest political crisis in more than a decade.
On Friday evening, President Santiago Peña was impeached after attempting to resign, and his vice president, Pedro Alliana, was sworn in as his replacement.
Authorities quickly arrested Peña, an economist and close ally of US President Donald Trump, and prosecutors charged him on Saturday with breach of trust and administration for personal gain. A judge ordered him held in pretrial detention at a military facility.
Peña has denied wrongdoing and his attorney, Ricardo Preda, told journalists that he was pleading not guilty to the charges.
The scandal has triggered public protests and sharp rebukes from the opposition.
“We are facing the biggest corruption scandal in our democratic history,” said opposition Senator Rafael Filizzola on Friday. “This impeachment is a first step toward ensuring justice is served.”
Manuel Ferreira, a Paraguayan economist and former finance minister, echoed much of the public anger over the case. “This was a modern-day Bonnie and Clyde,” he said. “They didn’t rob us with a pistol, they robbed us with an app. The head of the gang was the president of the republic.”
Until March 2025, Peña had been a business partner of the group that owns ueno. After his election in 2023, he tapped ueno’s former president, Carlos Carvallo, to lead the central bank.
Carvallo resigned as central bank chief earlier this week. Prosecutors charged him on Saturday with breach of trust, producing false public documents and administration for personal gain. They sought his pretrial detention, which was approved by a judge.
Carvallo did not respond to a request for comment. It was not immediately clear if he had entered a plea in the case.
Peña’s lawyer, Preda, objected to the impeachment, saying that ousting a president during a bank resolution could itself be destabilizing.
“What sets a serious country apart is not that its banks don’t fail, but how it responds,” Preda said on Friday. “If there is one thing that undermines confidence in the financial system, it is attempting to oust the president without evidence.”
Ueno was launched in 2021 as a sleek, millennial-friendly banking app that quickly won over Paraguayans who had been underserved by brick-and-mortar institutions.
It soon became deeply embedded in Paraguay’s payments system. It paired its digital offering with physical branches, later sponsoring sports teams, businesses and events. As of June, public institutions — including Paraguay’s state pension fund — held roughly $850 million in accounts with the bank.
But in recent months, internal regulatory reports warning of excessive lending to certain companies were leaked to local media outlets ABC and Última Hora, triggering political scrutiny of the bank’s lending practices.
Following growing public pressure, Paraguay’s central bank on Tuesday put ueno into resolution — its strongest measure short of immediate liquidation — after determining that ueno had breached minimum solvency requirements, locking millions of customers temporarily out of their accounts.
The central bank said on Saturday that the equivalent of $160 million had since been paid out to nearly 1.2 million savers under the state deposit guarantee scheme.
Authorities have promised that depositors will be reimbursed and say the crisis is confined to ueno. But analysts say the damage to Paraguay’s reputation as a stable investment destination in South America may linger far longer than the bank resolution itself.
“This is the moment when Paraguay must demonstrate that its institutions are functioning,” Ferreira said.
Published on November 9, 2026

sources.title: Paraguay’s Peña under house arrest as bank collapse ends presidency
sources.text:
Paraguay’s Peña under house arrest as bank collapse ends presidency
Pedro Alliana takes office after Ueno Bank’s failure freezes millions of customers’ savings and triggers investigations into public funds
- Santiago Peña placed under house arrest after Paraguay’s Senate removes him over the Ueno Bank crisis.
- Nearly 3 million customers lose access to their money as investigators examine lending irregularities and public deposits.
- Pedro Alliana takes over as president, facing demands to reimburse savers and restore confidence.
Paraguay’s ousted president Santiago Peña has been placed under house arrest after a banking scandal brought down his government within four days, leaving millions of customers unable to access their savings and exposing the scale of public money held by the failed lender.
Peña was detained at his home on Friday, 6 November, hours after the Senate removed him from office over the collapse of Ueno Bank. Vice-president Pedro Alliana was sworn in as his successor and will complete the presidential term ending in August 2028.
The Senate voted 44–0 to dismiss Peña for misconduct in office. His removal followed a unanimous impeachment vote in the lower house on Thursday, after Congress declined to accept his offer to resign.
Peña, who denies wrongdoing, faces investigations into suspected breach of trust, influence peddling and the use of public office for personal gain. Lawmakers accuse him of directing substantial public deposits towards a bank with which he had business connections.
The crisis erupted on Tuesday, 3 November, when the central bank took control of Ueno after discovering a severe capital shortfall. Its intervention halted banking services, leaving nearly 3 million customers unable to withdraw cash, use their cards or transfer money.
What began as a regulatory intervention rapidly became a political emergency. Depositors gathered outside shuttered branches, while demonstrators marched through Asunción demanding their savings and accountability from the government.
Ueno had expanded from a small finance company into one of Paraguay’s largest deposit-taking institutions. Its digital services and supermarket discounts attracted customers on low incomes, including many who had previously lacked access to banking.
The bank also became a significant custodian of state money. In October, it reported holding about $800 million in public deposits, including funds belonging to the state pension and health system and operators of Paraguay’s hydroelectric dams.
According to the central bank, investigators discovered inadequately documented loans to businesses connected to Ueno’s owners, alongside expenditure incorrectly recorded as assets. Correcting those entries left the bank’s capital below half the required minimum.
Regulators had warned the lender in June about its exposure to related companies. Fitch Ratings subsequently revised its outlook to negative in October, citing rapid expansion and a high proportion of intangible assets.
Peña’s relationship with the bank became central to the impeachment proceedings. A former International Monetary Fund economist, he held a stake in Grupo Vázquez, the conglomerate behind Ueno, until selling it in March 2025.
Lawmakers also challenged his appointment of Carlos Carvallo, a former head of Ueno’s predecessor, as central bank governor. The regulator has said Carvallo withdrew from decisions concerning the lender.
The accusations extend to the placement of $355 million in state pension money at Ueno, which lawmakers say exceeded legal limits. Investigators are examining whether officials failed to act on warning signs or concealed the bank’s difficulties.
Peña had publicly defended Ueno in October, arguing that a regulatory investigation did not mean it would close. He has since pledged to cooperate with investigators.
His political position collapsed when the ruling Colorado party withdrew its support. Horacio Cartes, the former president and party leader who helped Peña rise to power, distanced himself after the bank’s failure. Both principal Colorado factions in the lower house backed impeachment.
Peña sent lawyers to the Senate proceedings rather than attending himself. Senators rejected his request for an additional 72 hours to prepare his defence. He argued that receiving a lengthy indictment and hundreds of pages of supporting material shortly before the hearing denied him adequate preparation time.
The decision to pursue impeachment rather than accept his resignation also had legal consequences. Under Paraguay’s constitutional arrangements, resignation would have allowed Peña to become a senator for life, carrying parliamentary immunity that could have complicated prosecution.
He is the second Paraguayan president removed through impeachment since the dictatorship of Alfredo Stroessner ended in 1989. Fernando Lugo was dismissed in 2012.
For depositors, the immediate concern remains recovering their money. Deposit insurance covers balances up to approximately 228 million guaraníes, or $35,000, per person. The central bank says that protection covers 97 per cent of Ueno’s customers.
Payments began on Thursday with accounts holding up to 10 million guaraníes, approximately $1,500. The state pension fund has said pensions will continue as usual and transferred roughly 32,000 recipients who used Ueno to another bank.
The disruption has spread to businesses and public projects. A ride-hailing service dependent on Ueno suspended operations, affecting about 3,000 drivers. The state electricity company reported that $21 million intended for infrastructure works was trapped at the lender.
Criminal proceedings are also advancing against bank executives. Prosecutors have charged 27 people in a separate investigation, including founder and former chief executive Miguel Vázquez. Six former directors have been ordered into pretrial detention, while authorities have seized vehicles and other assets linked to him.
An arrest warrant was also issued for Carvallo, who resigned as central bank chief during the crisis. His custody status was not immediately clear.
Alliana inherits both the financial emergency and political scrutiny. He is himself under investigation in connection with the bank, although the lower house declined to initiate impeachment proceedings against him.
The central bank maintains that Ueno’s failure is an isolated event and that the wider financial system remains secure. For the new administration, returning customers’ money and explaining how public funds became so heavily exposed will be immediate tests of its authority.
With agency inputs

sources.title: Paraguay
sources.text:
Paraguay, officially the Republic of Paraguay, is a landlocked country located in the central region of South America. It borders Bolivia to the northwest and north, Brazil to the northeast and east, and Argentina to the southeast, south, and west. Paraguay has access to the Atlantic Ocean via the Paraná–Paraguay Waterway, a system of navigable channels shared by five countries. The country is governed as a unitary presidential republic composed of a capital district and seventeen departments. Its capital and largest city is Asunción. It dates its independence from Spain to 1811.
The indigenous Guaraní had been living in eastern Paraguay for at least a millennium before the arrival of Spanish conquistadores in 1524. The city of Asunción was founded in 1537 as the first capital of the Governorate of the Río de la Plata within the Spanish Empire. During the 17th century, Paraguay was the center of Jesuit missions, where the natives were converted to Christianity and introduced to European culture. After the expulsion of the Jesuits from Spanish territories in 1767, Paraguay increasingly became a peripheral colony. 
Following independence from Spain in the early 19th century, Paraguay was ruled by a series of authoritarian governments. This period ended with the disastrous Triple Alliance War (1864–1870), during which the country lost half its prewar population and around 25–33% of its territory. Paraguay prevailed in another major conflict in the twentieth century, the Chaco War with Bolivia (1932-1935). It subsequently came under a succession of military dictators, culminating in the 35-year regime of Alfredo Stroessner. He was overthrown in 1989 by an internal military coup, marking the beginning of Paraguay's current democratic era.
Paraguay is a developing country, ranking 99th in the Human Development Index, with the seventh highest GDP (PPP) per capita in South America. As of 2024, it had one of the fastest growing economies in the Western Hemisphere, driven by beef and soybean exports, manufacturing, and construction. Paraguay is one of the world's leading exporters of hydroelectricity; the Itaipu Dam on the Paraná River border with Brazil is the third-largest hydroelectric dam in the world in terms of produced energy. Paraguay is a founding member of Mercosur, the United Nations, the Organization of American States and the Lima Group. Additionally, the city of Luque, in metropolitan Asunción, is the seat of the South American Football Confederation. Ciudad del Este is Paraguay's second-largest city and hosts many of the country's consulates-general.
The majority of Paraguay's 6 million people are mestizo, and Guarani culture remains widely influential; more than 90% of the population speak various dialects of the Guarani language alongside Spanish, the highest rate of fluency in an indigenous language in Latin America. In a 2014 Positive Experience Index based on global polling data, Paraguay ranked as the "world's happiest place", and in 2024, placed 24th in the progress rankings of the World Happiness Report.


== Etymology ==
The origin of the word "Paraguay" is uncertain. One version postulates that the name is from the Guaraní language paraguá ("feather crown") and y ("water"): thus, paraguaí ("feather crown of waters"). Other versions state that the name derives from the Guaraní name for the Paraguay River, Payaguá-y ("river of the Payaguá people"). Yet another version states that the names comes from the Guaraní words para ("sea") + gua ("originates") + y ("river"): thus, "sea which originates from the river".


== History ==


=== Pre-colonial era ===
The indigenous Guaraní had been living in eastern Paraguay for at least a millennium before the arrival of the Spanish. Western Paraguay, the Gran Chaco, was inhabited by nomads of whom the Guaycuru peoples were the most prominent. The Paraguay River was roughly the dividing line between the agricultural Guarani people to the east and the nomadic and seminomadic people to the west in the Gran Chaco. The Mbayá nomads were known for their warrior traditions and were not fully pacified until the late 19th century. These indigenous tribes belonged to five distinct language families, which were the bases of their major divisions. Differing language speaking groups were generally competitive over resources and territories. They were further divided into tribes by speaking languages in branches of these families. Today 17 separate ethnolinguistic groups remain.


=== Colonial era ===
The first Europeans in the area were Spanish explorers in 1537. The Spanish explorer Juan de Salazar de Espinosa founded the settlement of Asunción on 15 August 1537. The city eventually became the center of a Spanish colonial province of Paraguay.
An attempt to create an autonomous Christian Indian nation was undertaken by Jesuit missions and settlements in this part of South America in the eighteenth century. They developed Jesuit reductions to bring Guarani populations together at Spanish missions and protect them from virtual slavery by Spanish settlers and Portuguese slave raiders, the bandeirantes, in addition to seeking their conversion to Christianity. Catholicism in Paraguay was influenced by the indigenous peoples: The syncretic religion has absorbed native elements. The reducciones flourished in eastern Paraguay for about 150 years, until the expulsion of the Jesuits by the Spanish Crown in 1767. The Jesuits were suppressed partially due to accusations by various European royal houses of prioritizing poor natives over Imperial interests. The ruins of two 18th century Jesuit Missions of La Santísima Trinidad de Paraná and Jesús de Tavarangue have been designated as World Heritage Sites by UNESCO.
In western Paraguay, Spanish settlement and Christianity were strongly resisted by the nomadic Guaycuru and other nomads from the 16th century onward. Most of these peoples were absorbed into the mestizo population in the 18th and 19th centuries.


=== Independence and rule of Rodríguez de Francia ===

Paraguay overthrew the local Spanish administration on 14 May 1811. Paraguay's first dictator was José Gaspar Rodríguez de Francia, who ruled Paraguay from 1814 until his death in 1840 with very little outside contact or influence. He intended to create a utopian society based on the Genevan theorist Jean-Jacques Rousseau's Social Contract. Rodríguez de Francia was nicknamed El Supremo.
Rodríguez de Francia established new laws that greatly reduced the powers of the Catholic church (Catholicism was then an established state religion) and the cabinet, forbade colonial citizens from marrying one another and allowed them to marry only blacks, mulattoes or natives, in order to break the power of colonial-era elites and to create a mixed-race or mestizo society. He cut off relations between Paraguay and the rest of South America. Because of Francia's restrictions of freedom, Fulgencio Yegros and several other Independence-era leaders in 1820 planned a coup d'état against Francia, who discovered the plot and had its leaders either executed or imprisoned for life.


=== Rule of the López family ===

After Francia's death in 1840, Paraguay was ruled by various military officers under a new junta militar, until Carlos Antonio López (allegedly Rodríguez de Francia's nephew) came to power in 1841. López modernized Paraguay and opened it to foreign commerce. He signed a nonaggression pact with Argentina and officially declared independence of Paraguay in 1842. After López's death in 1862, power was transferred to his eldest son, Francisco Solano López.
The regime of the López family was characterized by pervasive and rigid centralism in production and distribution. There was no distinction between the public and the private spheres, and the López family ruled the country as it would a large estate.
The government exerted control on all exports. The export of yerba mate and valuable wood products maintained the balance of trade between Paraguay and the outside world. The Paraguayan government was extremely protectionist, never accepted loans from abroad and levied high tariffs against imported foreign products. This protectionism made the society self-sufficient, and it also avoided the debt suffered by Argentina and Brazil. Slavery existed in Paraguay, although not in great numbers, until 1844, when it was legally abolished in the new constitution.
Francisco Solano López, the son of Carlos Antonio López, replaced his father as the President-Dictator in 1862, and generally continued the political policies of his father. Both wanted to give an international image of Paraguay as "democratic and republican", but in fact, the ruling family had almost total control of all public life in the country, including church and colleges.
Militarily, Carlos Antonio López modernized and expanded industry and the Paraguayan Army and greatly strengthened the strategic defenses of Paraguay by developing the Fortress of Humaitá. The government hired more than 200 foreign technicians, who installed telegraph lines and railroads to aid the expanding steel, textile, paper and ink, naval construction, weapons and gunpowder industries. The Ybycuí foundry, completed in 1850, manufactured cannons, mortars and bullets of all calibers. River warships were built in the shipyards of Asunción. Fortifications were built, especially along the Apa River and in Gran Chaco. Following the death of Carlos Antonio López, these projects continued under his son Francisco Solano.
In terms of socio-economic development, the country was dubbed "the most advanced Republic in South America", notably by the British judge and politician Sir Robert Phillimore.
According to George Thompson, Lieutenant Colonel of Engineers in the Paraguayan Army prior to and during the war, López's government was comparatively a good one for Paraguay:

Probably in no other country in the world has life and property been so secure as all over Paraguay during his (Antonio Lopez's) reign. Crime was almost unknown, and when committed, immediately detected and punished. The mass of the people was, perhaps, the happiest in existence. They had hardly to do any work to gain a livelihood. Each family had its house or hut in its own ground. They planted, in a few days, enough tobacco, maize and mandioca for their own consumption [...]. Having at every hut a grove of oranges [...] and also a few cows, they were almost throughout the year under little necessity [...]. The higher classes, of course, lived more in the European way...


=== Paraguayan War (1864–1870) ===

On 12 October 1864, despite Paraguayan ultimatums, Brazil (allied with the Argentine Government under General Bartolomé Mitre and the rebellious Uruguayan colorados led by Gen. Venancio Flores) invaded the Republic of Uruguay in order to overthrow the government of that time (which was under the rule of the Blanco Party, an ally of López), The Paraguayans, in turn, led by the Marshal of the Republic Francisco Solano López, attacked Mato Grosso on 15 December 1864 and later declared war against Argentina on 23 March 1865. The Blanco Government was toppled and replaced by a Colorado government under General Venancio Flores on 22 February 1865. Afterward, the Argentine Republic, the Empire of Brazil and the Republic of Uruguay signed the secret Treaty of the Triple Alliance against the Paraguayan Government on 1 May 1865.
After a brief offensive in Argentine and Brazilian territory, the Paraguayans retreated to national territory where they put up a ferocious resistance. With the capture of Asunción, the Triple Alliance installed a provisional government. On 22 July 1869 the National Assembly elected the National Junta formed by Carlos Loizaga, Juan Francisco Decoud and Cirilo Antonio Rivarola. sources.title: Afonso Pena
sources.text:
Afonso Augusto Moreira Pena (30 November 1847 – 14 June 1909) was a Brazilian lawyer, professor, and politician who served as the sixth president of Brazil, from 1906 until his death in 1909. Pena was elected in 1906, the chosen successor of president Rodrigues Alves. Pena was the first politician from Minas Gerais to win the presidency, ending the series of politicians from São Paulo who had held the presidency since 1894. Before his presidency, he served as the 4th vice president of Brazil, under Rodrigues Alves (1903–1906) after the death of Silviano Brandão. Pena was a monarchist. He was the only member of Emperor Pedro II's cabinet to become president of Brazil and the first Brazilian president to die in office.
Pena was born in Santa Bárbara, Minas Gerais, in 1847. His father, Domingos José Teixeira Pena, was a Portuguese immigrant who owned slaves and a gold mine. After graduating with a law degree from the Faculty of Law of São Paulo and becoming a doctor at the same institution, Pena returned to his hometown, where he began to work as an attorney, later moving to Barbacena and becoming known for defending slaves. His political career began in 1874 when he joined the Liberal Party and was elected to the Provincial Assembly of Minas Gerais. In 1878, he was elected general deputy for Minas Gerais. In the succeeding years he reconciled legislative work with some periods occupying ministries—Ministry of War (1882), Agriculture (1883–1884), and Justice (1885).
After the proclamation of the Republic, Pena withdrew from public life; however, he was soon called upon to join the Republican Party of Minas Gerais (PRM) and run for the State Senate in order to help with the creation of the new state constitution. Pena was elected to the position in 1891 and presided over the commission that was tasked with drafting the constitution. After resigning his position in the Senate, Pena was elected president of Minas Gerais by consensus among the state's various political factions, serving from 1892 to 1894. It was during his administration that Belo Horizonte was established as the future state capital (which at that time was Ouro Preto) and the Faculty of Law of Minas Gerais was founded. After presiding over the Bank of the Republic from 1895 to 1898, Pena became vice president to Rodrigues Alves in 1903. As vice president, he also served as president of the Senate.
Pena became president of Brazil in 1906 after an uncontested single-candidate election. He was the first Brazilian president to intervene in the coffee economy, putting into practice the Taubaté Agreement, after which the federal government began to buy surplus production in order to maintain the high price of coffee in international markets. Pena's government promoted the expansion of railways and immigration, the modernization and reorganization of the Brazilian Army with the introduction of the Sortition Law, and the rearmament of the Brazilian Navy, with the acquisition of new ships. Pena also supported Cândido Rondon's expeditions in the Amazon rainforest, which linked the region to Rio de Janeiro by telegraph. In the international sphere, Brazil took part in the Hague Convention of 1907, with a delegation led by Ruy Barbosa, and settled border disputes with neighboring countries. Tensions with Argentina reached a peak due to Brazil's acquisition of the Minas Geraes-class battleships, which provoked the South American dreadnought race, and both countries hovered on the brink of war. In his final years in office, Pena unsuccessfully tried to nominate David Campista as his successor. Pena died from severe pneumonia in 1909 and was succeeded by Nilo Peçanha.


== Early life and education ==

Born on 30 November 1847 in Santa Bárbara do Mato Dentro—currently the municipality of Santa Bárbara, Minas Gerais—Afonso Pena was the seventh of twelve children of Domingos José Teixeira Penna and Anna Moreira Teixeira Penna; being his mother's firstborn, as she was his father's second wife. Domingos was a Portuguese immigrant from São Salvador da Ribeira de Pena (also spelled "da Penha") and in the new country he owned land, a gold mine, and a large number of slaves. Domingos' father, Manuel José de Carvalho Penha (b. 1769), was supposedly the first to adopt the name "Pena".
While initially pursuing a military career in the National Guard, Domingos later abandoned it; his earnings were sufficient to provide the family with a standard of living described as "comfortable". Afonso's mother came from an influential family in Santa Bárbara politics. Thus, Afonso's family was part of Minas Gerais' elite. As a child, he was taken care of by the nursemaid Ambrosina, a slave. Pena would often accompany his father to the gold mines in Brumado and São Gonçalo do Rio Abaixo. According to José Anchieta da Silva, Pena was an early abolitionist who fought for better working conditions for his father's slaves; on one occasion, upon seeing a pregnant slave working in a mine, Pena spoke to the overseer, after which it was decided that pregnant slaves would no longer work in the mines from the sixth month of pregnancy onwards, and their only task would be "to cook or wash clothes".
After receiving his early education at home from private tutors, Pena went on to study at the Caraça School in 1857, at the age of ten. The school, isolated from major urban centers, was maintained by the Lazarist priests, and Pena's father was one of its most prominent creditors. At the school, he studied theology, ethics, philosophy, mathematics, geometry, history, rhetoric, and foreign languages. Pena finished his studies at the Caraça School on 16 January 1864 and later moved to the city of São Paulo to study at the Faculty of Law in 1866, which, together with the Faculty of Law of Recife, formed the country's intelligentsia at the time.


=== At the Faculty of Law ===

During his studies at the Faculty of Law, Pena was a colleague of Ruy Barbosa, Bias Fortes, Joaquim Nabuco, Castro Alves, and Rodrigues Alves. In 1870 Pena became, alongside Rodrigues Alves, an editor in chief of the faculty's journal Imprensa Acadêmica after a close election. There was supposed to be only one editor in chief, but the election unexpectedly ended in a tie. It was then agreed to include both Pena and Alves as chief editors. The journal, focused on debating academic and political issues, was influenced by French authors such as Victor Hugo, Honoré de Balzac, and Émile Zola.
Although not a freemason, he joined the Bucha in the Faculty of Law—a secret student society of a liberal, abolitionist, and republican nature, which was inspired by the German Burschenschaft associations and founded by professor Julius Frank—and became chief of Bucha's "General Communion". This association helped students who could not afford to pay for their studies. Pena maintained contact with other Bucha members, even after finishing his studies at the faculty.
Pena was an adherent of natural law and an opponent of positivism, as he was a fervent Catholic and sympathetic to the monarchy in Brazil. His ideas distanced him from the Brazilian positivists, who defended the separation of Church and State and the creation of a military republic in the country. Two other movements divided Brazil during his years at the Faculty of Law: abolitionism and republicanism. Pena supported the former but not the latter, refusing to sign the 1870 Republican Manifesto, as he believed Brazil was not ready for a change of regime.


=== Early law career ===

Pena graduated with a Law degree on 23 October 1870. He became a Doctor of Law at the same institution on 29 August 1871 – the only one in his class – after defending his thesis Letra de Câmbio on 19 June of that year. Upon receiving his doctorate, Pena gave a speech in which he expressed his abolitionist views, concluding that "the entire country is agitated to solve, in accordance with the principles of justice, the great question of the centuries – the emancipation of an enslaved race". After turning down an invitation to teach at his alma mater, he returned to Minas Gerais, where he began to work as an attorney, at first practicing law in his hometown and later in Barbacena.
There he became known for defending slaves in court and even for helping them escape, for which he came close to being repported to the authorities in Rio de Janeiro by a local military officer. Despite this, he was concerned with the economic effects that immediate abolition could have; for this reason, he was in favor of compensating slave owners after abolition and also supported immigration as a way to replace slave labor. This brought him closer to other politicians of his time, especially the conservatives, who, according to Cláudia Viscardi, were "responsible for the progressive delay of the end of slavery in Brazil".


=== Marriage and family ===
Afonso Pena married Maria Guilhermina de Oliveira on 23 January 1875. The couple went on their honeymoon to Rio de Janeiro, where they met emperor Pedro II. Guilhermina was the daughter of João Fernandes de Oliveira Pena, the Viscount of Carandaí, and the niece of Honório Hermeto Carneiro Leão, the Marquis of Paraná, one of the most prominent politicians in the Empire of Brazil. They had nine children, including Afonso Júnior, who was later Minister of Justice and Internal Affairs under President Artur Bernardes and a member of the Brazilian Academy of Letters, and Octávio Moreira Pena, an engineer who carried out several public works in Rio de Janeiro, including the landfill that gave rise to the Urca neighborhood.
Pena inherited properties from his parents, including a gold mine, which he sold by the end of the 19th century, as its gold production had declined. He also had a textile factory, which he sold in the 1900s, as well as several investments in Brazil and abroad. In order to better manage his investments, Pena was helped by João Ribeiro de Oliveira Sousa, who became president of Crédito Real, then Minas Gerais' largest bank, on Pena's recommendation.


== Political rise ==


=== Member of parliament (1874–1882) ===

Afonso Pena joined the Liberal Party in 1874 and began his political career that same year, when he was elected provincial deputy to the 20th legislature in Minas Gerais. He remained in the Provincial Assembly until 1878, being successively reelected to the 21st (1876–1877) and 22nd (1878–1879) legislatures, when he was elected general deputy, beginning his term in the Chamber of Deputies in the 17th legislature (1878–1881). Pena's political career was initially sponsored by Martinho Campos and Afonso Celso, two prominent politicians who helped him in his rise in the Liberal Party.
The liberals' rise to power in 1878 came after a decade in ostracism (the so-called Conservative Decade), being tasked by the emperor with carrying out an electoral reform to establish direct voting. The party's rise to power had not resulted from its own political strength, and Pena warned his fellow Liberals of its unstable position. The new liberal prime minister, João Lins Cansanção, was out of step with the party's mainstream, leaving a pessimistic impression on Pena. The issue of direct voting, the main point of the liberal program, was the subject of debates about which path should be adopted: a constitutional reform or the approval of an ordinary law. Most liberals were in favor of a constitutional reform, which would require deliberation by the Senate, where there was a conservative majority. Pena was against this path, joining a dissident wing within the party.
Cansanção fell on 28 March 1880, as desired by Pena. His successor, also liberal José Antônio Saraiva, then decided to carry out the electoral reform by means of an ordinary law. The Saraiva Law, as it became known, was finally approved on 9 January 1881, introducing direct voting in Brazil, the voter's license, and allowing non-Catholics to vote.
